meta.title: Why a rocket points into the wind
meta.footer: Minerva BR-1 build day  ·  Georgia Wing High Power Rocketry
meta.description: Why a rocket with its CP behind its CG straightens itself after a gust, and why one with the CP in front comes around and dives. A weather vane, then the three pushes on a rocket.
credits: Sequence after "Rocket Stability" by Angelo State University Engineering (public domain), youtu.be/pnY5hkmJS58; redrawn for the BR-1
Weather vane: Rooster Weathervane, 19th century, sheet and wrought iron, Smithsonian American Art Museum 1986.65.366 (CC0, Smithsonian Open Access)
BR-1 geometry, CG and CP: the program's OpenRocket file (files/BR-1.ork), designed by Michael Bright

cues.title: Why a rocket points into the wind
cues.sub: The air pushes at the CP. The rocket pivots at the CG. Put the CP behind, and every gust straightens the rocket.
cues.say: Why a rocket points into the wind. By the end of this you will be able to explain why a rocket with its CP behind its CG straightens itself out after a gust, and what happens when the CP is in front.

cues.heading: Start with a weather vane
cues.say: Start with a weather vane. It is a rocket's simplest cousin. It turns on a rod, and the rod goes through its balance point, the center of gravity. Its tail is a big flat plate. A big flat plate catches a lot of air, so the point where the air pushes, the center of pressure, sits back in the tail. Pivot in the middle, push at the back. Hold that picture.

cues.heading: A push behind the pivot
cues.say: Now the wind shifts. The air pushes on the vane at the CP, in the direction the wind is blowing. The rod pushes back at the pivot, the CG. Two pushes, equal and opposite, but no longer on the same line. Two pushes that miss each other make a twist. Engineers call it a moment, or torque. The twist swings the tail downwind and the nose upwind, until the two pushes line up again. That is all a weather vane is. A push behind a pivot always points the thing into the wind.

cues.heading: Three pushes on a rocket
cues.say: Now the BR-1 in front of you, in flight. Three pushes act on it. Its weight pulls down at the CG. The air rushing past drags on it, and that drag acts at the CP. The motor's thrust pushes up from the tail. Flying straight, all three sit on one line, straight up the middle of the rocket, and nothing twists. The rocket climbs true.

cues.question: A gust hits the rocket from the side. Which point does it turn around?

lines: Anything free in the air spins about its balance point
The vane's rod sat at its CG for the same reason
The CG is the pivot. The CP is the push
cues.say: The CG. Anything moving freely through the air spins about its balance point. The weather vane turned on its rod because the rod went through its CG. A rocket has no rod, so it pivots around its balance point in mid-air. That is why the two dots matter so much. The CG is the pivot. The CP is where the air pushes. Whether the push is behind the pivot or in front of it decides what the twist does.

cues.heading: CP behind: the gust fixes itself
cues.say: Here is the BR-1 with its fins on. The CP is behind the CG, near the fins. A gust tips the nose over. Now the air is not rushing straight down the rocket. It hits the side, and the drag at the CP grows and swings sideways. That push is behind the pivot, like the vane's tail. The twist turns the nose back into the airflow. The rocket straightens out on its own, within a second, and keeps climbing. It is a weather vane with a motor.

cues.heading: CP in front: the gust wins
cues.say: Now take the fins off. The center of pressure segment showed that the CP moves forward without them, and here it lands ahead of the CG. Same gust, same tip. The drag still grows at the CP, but now that push is in front of the pivot. The twist tips the nose further over, not back. It keeps going. The rocket comes around, and with the motor still burning, the thrust drives it toward the ground. Nothing about the motor changed. Only where the push sits compared with the pivot.

cues.heading: Behind, and by how much
lines: CP behind the CG: every gust straightens the rocket
CP in front: every gust grows
How far behind is enough: Stability margin, next
cues.note: Fins are at the back for one reason: to put the CP behind the pivot.
cues.say: So the rule has a reason now. CP behind the CG, and every gust straightens the rocket. CP in front, and every gust grows until the rocket comes around. That is why the fins are at the back of every rocket on this table, from the Alpha III you built this morning to the BR-1. They put the CP behind the pivot. How far behind is enough, and how the program checks it, is the next segment, Stability margin.

cues.text: The air pushes at the CP. The rocket pivots at the CG. Keep the CP behind the CG, and every gust straightens the rocket.
cues.say: The one thing to remember. The air pushes at the CP. The rocket pivots at the CG. Keep the CP behind the CG, and every gust straightens the rocket instead of tipping it.
